additions.title: Verification lab: commit to deployed response
additions.content_value:
# Verification lab: prove which commit reached your cluster

This lab strengthens the existing Linux → Git → Jenkins → Docker → Kubernetes sequence with observable acceptance checks. Keep the linked recordings and parameterized project alongside it. The goal is an evidence chain: a source revision, a passing check, an identified image, and the response from the deployed application.

## Prerequisites and study sequence

Use a practice directory, Python 3, Git with a configured author identity, Docker, kubectl, and an existing local Minikube installation. Container and cluster steps need a working container runtime and downloaded images; the Python checks run independently. Record tool versions and the current kubectl context. Use a dedicated local learning cluster.

First complete the Linux lessons and explain paths, exit status, and environment variables. Next make a Git change and inspect its diff. Study the Jenkins lessons before automating that check. Finally build the container, inspect it locally, and repeat the same acceptance check through Kubernetes. Registry publication is an extension once local delivery works.

A Jenkinsfile describes stages; its agent still needs the tools and permissions those stages call. Scope registry credentials to the push stage and use Jenkins credential IDs. A pull request from an untrusted contributor must not receive deployment credentials. See the [Jenkinsfile documentation](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/pipeline/jenkinsfile/) for stage execution and credential handling.

## Runnable exercise: a release with an identity

Create these files in the practice directory. The application returns its revision and has a separate health endpoint.

`app.py`:

```python
import os
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

def route(path, revision):
    if path == '/health':
        return 200, b'ok\n'
    if path == '/':
        return 200, f'revision={revision}\n'.encode()
    return 404, b'not found\n'

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        status, body = route(self.path, os.environ.get('SOURCE_REV', 'dev'))
        self.send_response(status)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    HTTPServer(('0.0.0.0', 8080), Handler).serve_forever()
```

`test_app.py`:

```python
import unittest
from app import route

class ReleaseContract(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_release_identity(self):
        self.assertEqual(route('/', 'commit123'), (200, b'revision=commit123\n'))
        self.assertNotEqual(route('/', 'commit123'), route('/', 'commit456'))
    def test_health_and_unknown_route(self):
        self.assertEqual(route('/health', 'commit123'), (200, b'ok\n'))
        self.assertEqual(route('/missing', 'commit123')[0], 404)
```

Run `python3 -m unittest -v`: expect two passing tests. These check the release response, the health contract, and missing-route behavior. They complement the HTTP smoke test below; they do not establish deployment correctness by themselves.

Create a `Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
ARG SOURCE_REV=dev
ENV SOURCE_REV=$SOURCE_REV
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.revision=$SOURCE_REV
WORKDIR /app
COPY app.py test_app.py ./
RUN python -m unittest -v
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

Commit the files, then build and inspect the application:

```bash
git init
git add app.py test_app.py Dockerfile
git commit -m 'Add release identity and contract checks'
revision=$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)
docker build --build-arg SOURCE_REV="$revision" -t "kg-cicd:$revision" .
docker run --rm --name kg-cicd-check -p 127.0.0.1:18080:8080 "kg-cicd:$revision"
```

Leave the container running. In a second terminal, `curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:18080/health` must print `ok`; requesting `/` must print the twelve-character revision after `revision=`. Stop the container before continuing. The [Docker build guide](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/) explains build context and image construction; for a release pipeline, record the resolved base-image and application-image digests as well as tags.

With the local learning cluster selected, repeat through Kubernetes:

```bash
minikube image load "kg-cicd:$revision"
kubectl create deployment kg-cicd --image="kg-cicd:$revision" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl rollout status deployment/kg-cicd --timeout=120s
kubectl port-forward deployment/kg-cicd 18080:8080
```

Run the same curl checks in another terminal. Capture the Pod image ID and observed revision. Loading the image is necessary because your cluster does not automatically share the host's image store. A [Deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) manages rollout state; an HTTP response checks what the application actually serves.

## Failure experiment and Jenkins integration

Change the health test expectation to an incorrect value. The next Docker build must fail before producing a successful release. Restore the test, commit again, and build the new revision. Put `python3 -m unittest -v` before image publication in Jenkins, and keep the nonzero exit status intact: `|| true` would bypass this gate.

If a Pod reports ImagePullBackOff, inspect its events and image availability. If it starts but serves the wrong revision, compare tag, image ID, and build argument. If port forwarding fails, inspect Pod readiness and selected context before changing application code. Add a readiness probe in the capstone; [Kubernetes probe documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) distinguishes traffic readiness from process liveness.

## Capstone and evidence rubric

Submit a repository and a one-page run record. Award 25% for meaningful checks and a demonstrated failing gate, 25% for commit-to-image traceability, 25% for the observed deployed response and readiness configuration, and 25% for recovery: a second release, controlled rollback, verified old response, and cleanup commands. A screenshot of a green job without the source revision or deployed response earns no traceability credit. Reproduce the workflow on another learner's local environment before calling it portable.

capsule_updates.description: Use a Jenkinsfile to make build steps reviewable with the application. Intentionally fail a check, confirm later delivery stages do not run, then restore it and compare the two build records; do not treat a green job as proof without inspecting what it tested.

Walk through a small change from an isolated branch to a reviewed commit and remote push. Inspect the diff before committing, capture the resulting commit ID, and explain how that ID should follow the change into its build artifact.

Describe continuous integration as an automated check of a specific revision, then map checkout, test, and build into Jenkins stages. Define which failures must stop the pipeline and preserve a log that identifies the failing stage and source commit.

Build confidence with paths, files, pipes, permissions, and exit codes before running deployment commands. Use the linked Linux resource to assemble a short command log that shows where a file lives, who can read it, and whether each command succeeded.

Complete a small deployment and verify it from outside the Pod using a Service or port forwarding. Record the image version, readiness result, and response body, then rehearse a controlled rollback and confirm which version is serving afterward.

Explain how a Deployment maintains Pods and how a Service selects their endpoints. Trace labels, selectors, image identity, and ports through a minimal application, then use rollout status and Pod events to verify the result.

Set up a practice repository and complete the add, commit, status, log, and push cycle. Verify the change on the remote and leave credentials outside committed files; use the linked recording alongside your own command transcript.

Practice a repeatable command-line investigation: inspect the current directory and environment, locate a process, read its logs, and check its exit status. Keep a small troubleshooting checklist so a failed build produces evidence rather than a sequence of guesses.

Distinguish your working tree, the staging area, and committed history, then connect a local repository to a GitHub remote. Use the linked guide to explain what is shared by a push and what remains only on your computer.

Connect a Jenkins job to the agent, workspace, parameters, and credentials it needs. Produce a short environment checklist: a pipeline definition alone does not install Python, Docker, kubectl, registry permissions, or access to a cluster.

Connect Linux processes, environment variables, and filesystem permissions to the machine that runs a delivery pipeline. Record how you would identify a running service, inspect its output, and diagnose a permission failure without relying on a graphical interface.

Implement the parameterized project with your own repository, registry, and local cluster settings. Use the added verification lab to test the application itself, identify the deployed revision, and demonstrate that a failed check prevents delivery before presenting your final pipeline.

Distinguish a Docker image from its running containers and Docker Hub from the local image store. Use your own registry namespace and a scoped access token, then verify that another environment can retrieve the intended image.

Turn the delivery workflow into an operational blueprint: prerequisites, stage inputs and outputs, credentials, failure gates, and recovery steps. Explain the boundary between automatically validating a change and deciding whether it should reach a particular environment.

Trace a single application change through Git, Jenkins, Docker, and Kubernetes using the linked implementation recording as a companion. Build an evidence chain from commit ID to image identity to deployed response, including the checks that can stop delivery.

Follow one image through build, local execution, and registry publication. Record its repository, tag, and digest, verify the exposed application response, and explain why rebuilding or reusing a mutable tag can change what another machine receives.

Use a local Minikube cluster to practice deployment without requiring a production account. Confirm the kubectl context and namespace, choose how the cluster obtains its image, and separate image-pull failures from application-startup failures.

Read a Dockerfile as an explicit description of runtime files and startup behavior. Identify the base image, build context, working directory, copied files, and process command, then check that the container works without depending on an unmounted file from your laptop.

quizzes.title: CI failure gates and delivery evidence

questions.question_text: A Jenkins test stage runs `python3 -m unittest -v || true`. A test fails, but the image is pushed and deployed. What is the most direct fix?

options.b: Preserve the test command’s nonzero exit status and require a successful test stage before publishing
options.c: Rename the Docker image to latest
options.d: Run the failing test only after deployment

questions.explanation: The shell fallback turns a failed check into a successful exit status. A delivery gate must retain the failure so later publishing and deployment steps do not run.

questions.question_text: The container starts, but the application serves an older revision. Which evidence most directly identifies what is running?

options.b: The fact that the Jenkins job is green
options.c: The running container’s image ID/digest together with the application’s revision response
options.d: The name of the Kubernetes namespace alone

questions.explanation: Source, build, and runtime are separate steps. Inspecting the actual image identity and served revision tests the connection between the intended artifact and the running application.

questions.question_text: A process is running but is not yet able to serve application requests. Which Kubernetes mechanism is intended to keep it out of ready Service endpoints?
questions.explanation: Readiness tells Kubernetes whether a container is prepared to receive traffic. It is different from checking whether a process is alive.

questions.question_text: After a controlled rollback, what is the strongest completion check for this lab?

options.a: The rollback command was typed without an error
options.b: The original developer says the earlier release worked
options.c: The tag still has the same name
options.d: Rollout status completes and a request through the deployed application returns the expected earlier revision

questions.explanation: A rollback request is an action, not evidence of the resulting application state. Verify both workload rollout and the response that users actually receive.

# End-to-End Project: Your Commit → Your Cluster

This guide is fully **parameterized** — set the variables below once, then every
command works for ANY user, on any machine. Nothing in this project is tied to
the instructor's accounts.

## 0. Your variables (set once)

```bash
export GITHUB_USER="<your-github-username>"
export DOCKERHUB_USER="<your-dockerhub-username>"
export APP_NAME="cicd-demo"
export IMAGE="$DOCKERHUB_USER/$APP_NAME"
export K8S_NAMESPACE="demo"
```

Put these in your shell profile (or a `.env` you `source`) so every step below
is copy-paste. Wherever a file cannot read your shell (Jenkinsfile, YAML), we
inject them explicitly — that is the whole trick that makes this repeatable.

## 1. The application repository

```bash
git init "$APP_NAME" && cd "$APP_NAME"
# app.py — a minimal web app; any language works, the pipeline is the point
cat > app.py <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200); self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b"pipeline works!")
HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), H).serve_forever()
PY
cat > test_app.py <<'PY'
def test_truth():
    assert 1 + 1 == 2
PY
git add -A && git commit -m "app + test"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin "git@github.com:$GITHUB_USER/$APP_NAME.git"
git push -u origin main
```

## 2. The Dockerfile

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY app.py .
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

```bash
docker build -t "$IMAGE:local" .
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 "$IMAGE:local" && curl localhost:8080
```

## 3. Jenkins credentials (one-time, per user)

In Jenkins → Manage Jenkins → Credentials, add:
- `dockerhub-creds` — your Docker Hub username + access token
- `github-creds` — your GitHub credentials (or use a public repo)

The Jenkinsfile refers to credentials **by these IDs**, never by value — that
is what lets every student use their own accounts unchanged.

## 4. The Jenkinsfile (parameterized)

```groovy
pipeline {
  agent any
  environment {
    IMAGE = "${env.DOCKERHUB_USER}/${env.APP_NAME}"
  }
  parameters {
    string(name: 'DOCKERHUB_USER', defaultValue: 'CHANGE-ME')
    string(name: 'APP_NAME', defaultValue: 'cicd-demo')
  }
  stages {
    stage('Test')  { steps { sh 'python -m pytest -q' } }
    stage('Build') { steps { sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE:$BUILD_NUMBER .' } }
    stage('Push')  {
      steps {
        withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'dockerhub-creds',
            usernameVariable: 'DH_USER', passwordVariable: 'DH_TOKEN')]) {
          sh 'echo "$DH_TOKEN" | docker login -u "$DH_USER" --password-stdin'
          sh 'docker push $IMAGE:$BUILD_NUMBER'
        }
      }
    }
    stage('Deploy') {
      steps {
        sh 'sed "s|__IMAGE__|$IMAGE:$BUILD_NUMBER|" k8s/deployment.yaml | kubectl apply -f -'
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Add a GitHub webhook: repo → Settings → Webhooks →
`http://<your-jenkins-host>/github-webhook/` — push events.

## 5. Kubernetes manifests (image is a placeholder)

`k8s/deployment.yaml`:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: cicd-demo }
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: cicd-demo } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: cicd-demo } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: __IMAGE__        # substituted by the pipeline — never hardcoded
          ports: [ { containerPort: 8080 } ]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: cicd-demo }
spec:
  selector: { app: cicd-demo }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 8080 } ]
  type: NodePort
```

```bash
minikube start
kubectl create namespace "$K8S_NAMESPACE" || true
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace="$K8S_NAMESPACE"
```

## 6. Run the loop

```bash
echo "# trigger" >> app.py
git commit -am "pipeline test" && git push
# webhook → Jenkins: Test → Build → Push → Deploy
kubectl get pods -w
minikube service cicd-demo -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE"
```

## 7. Checklist — proof it is user-agnostic

- [ ] No username appears in any committed file (only `$VARS` and `__IMAGE__`)
- [ ] A classmate can clone your repo, set THEIR variables, and deploy
- [ ] Rolling back is one command: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/cicd-demo`

additions.title: Planning baseline and closed-loop evaluation lab
additions.content_value:
# Planning lab: establish a baseline before adding learning

Use this guide across the existing programming notebooks, global-search tutorial, FSM, lattice, PPO, and uncertainty resources. The course remains early access: the separate PPO learning path currently has no attached lessons. This exercise supplies a complete classical baseline; it does not claim that every planned learned-planning topic has already shipped.

## Prerequisites and study sequence

You need Python 3 and familiarity with tuples, sets, dictionaries, loops, and functions. No additional package or GPU is needed for the exercise. Start with the Python and algorithms notebooks. Use the data-analysis and SQL material to organize results, then study the introduction lecture and presentation before modifying the planning examples.

Keep three interfaces separate: a route gives a spatial objective, a behavior chooses a maneuver, and a trajectory assigns motion over time. A grid path is an intentionally simplified route example. It has no steering limits, acceleration model, or dynamic obstacles. [LaValle's Planning Algorithms](https://lavalle.pl/planning/) develops the distinctions between discrete search, configuration space, and planning under differential constraints.

## Runnable exercise: a falsifiable A* implementation

Save this as `baseline.py` and run `python3 baseline.py`. Coordinates are integer `(x, y)` cells on a 6 × 6 grid. Each legal move changes one coordinate by one cell and costs one. The Manhattan heuristic is a lower bound under these movement assumptions.

```python
from heapq import heappop, heappush

START, GOAL = (0, 0), (5, 0)
def astar(blocked):
    if START in blocked or GOAL in blocked:
        return None
    heuristic = lambda p: abs(p[0]-GOAL[0]) + abs(p[1]-GOAL[1])
    queue = [(heuristic(START), 0, START)]
    cost, parent = {START: 0}, {}
    while queue:
        _, g, current = heappop(queue)
        if g != cost[current]:
            continue
        if current == GOAL:
            path = [current]
            while current != START:
                current = parent[current]
                path.append(current)
            return list(reversed(path))
        x, y = current
        for neighbor in [(x+1,y), (x-1,y), (x,y+1), (x,y-1)]:
            nx, ny = neighbor
            if not (0 <= nx < 6 and 0 <= ny < 6) or neighbor in blocked:
                continue
            new_cost = g + 1
            if new_cost < cost.get(neighbor, float('inf')):
                cost[neighbor], parent[neighbor] = new_cost, current
                heappush(queue, (new_cost + heuristic(neighbor), new_cost, neighbor))
    return None

wall = {(3, y) for y in range(5)}
path = astar(wall)
assert path is not None and len(path)-1 == 15
assert path[0] == START and path[-1] == GOAL
assert not any(p in wall for p in path)
assert all(abs(a[0]-b[0])+abs(a[1]-b[1]) == 1
           for a, b in zip(path, path[1:]))
assert astar(wall | {(3, 5)}) is None
print('open-gap cost:', len(path)-1)
print('closed-gap result:', astar(wall | {(3, 5)}))
```

Expect `open-gap cost: 15` and `closed-gap result: None`. The five-cell wall forces travel to the bottom gap and back up; closing its last cell disconnects the start and goal. The assertions check more than whether a path was drawn. Python's [heapq reference](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html) explains the minimum-priority queue used here.

Compare against the course A* notebook on the same map and movement rules. If costs disagree, inspect coordinate conventions, diagonal moves, obstacle inclusion, and path reconstruction before timing the algorithms. As an extension, use a zero heuristic and compare cost and expansion counts. An admissible heuristic need not produce the same tied path, but this fixed unit-cost problem should retain the same optimal cost.

## From point paths to decisions and trajectories

Now inflate each obstacle by one cell in all directions and clip to the map. The narrow gap closes. Explain why a route for a point is not automatically feasible for a vehicle footprint. This grid inflation is a teaching approximation; do not label it a complete vehicle collision model.

Next use the FSM notebook to write transition guards for cruise, follow, and stop. Replay a blocked lane and an oscillating distance estimate; log the state and guard at every step. Introduce a dwell condition or separate entry/exit thresholds and check whether unnecessary switching decreases without masking a genuine stop condition.

For the lattice lesson, record each candidate's collision result, clearance, duration, maximum acceleration, and selection cost. Compare candidates only after applying your declared feasibility constraints. A small scalar cost does not compensate for a collision or an infeasible actuator demand.

For the traffic project, read the existing [Intelligent Driver Model explanation](https://traffic-simulation.de/info/info_IDM.html). Identify desired speed, time headway, spacing, and acceleration assumptions before changing a parameter. Compare identical initial conditions with two simulation time steps and inspect minimum gap, not just the animation.

## Learned planning and uncertainty experiments

When a runnable PPO implementation is available, freeze the observation and action definitions and separate training seeds from evaluation seeds. The [original PPO paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347) describes a policy-optimization method; it is not a driving-safety guarantee. Evaluate a simple baseline and the learned policy on matching scenarios and report collisions, completion, and time taken separately from reward.

Include a lead vehicle that brakes, a blocked route, noisy state estimates, and an unfamiliar initial gap. Under uncertainty, record at least two plausible future trajectories and explain why the selected maneuver remains acceptable under the assumptions. If it does not, state the failure and the fallback rather than averaging it away.

## Capstone and evaluation rubric

Submit code, environment versions, scenario definitions, seeds, and a results table. Allocate 30% to search correctness and explicit infeasibility handling, 25% to behavior and trajectory interfaces with logged constraints, 25% to matched scenario evaluation including failures, and 20% to reproducibility and honest limitations. Compare classical and learned planners only where both actually run. A reward curve alone does not earn collision-evaluation credit. Keep all experiments in simulation and describe what additional vehicle modeling and validation would be needed before any physical deployment.

questions.question_text: On a four-connected grid with one-unit costs for horizontal and vertical moves, why is Manhattan distance an admissible A* heuristic?

options.a: It exactly predicts every obstacle detour
options.b: It never exceeds the obstacle-free minimum movement cost under these rules
options.c: It includes the vehicle steering dynamics
options.d: It remains admissible for any movement cost and any diagonal rule

questions.explanation: Changing one coordinate by one costs a unit, so at least |dx|+|dy| steps are needed without obstacles. Obstacles cannot shorten that minimum. Different movement rules require reconsidering the heuristic.

questions.question_text: In the lab, closing the only gap in the wall produces no valid path. What should the planner report?

options.a: An explicit unreachable/infeasible result under the current map and movement model
options.b: A straight line through the nearest obstacle
options.c: The last explored cell as a successful goal
options.d: A shorter path cost to encourage progress

questions.explanation: Failure to find a feasible route is a meaningful output. Fabricating a goal-reaching path would hide a broken safety or validity assumption.

questions.question_text: A route avoids occupied grid cells, but the vehicle body overlaps an obstacle while following it. What assumption was missing?

options.a: That the path should have more plotted points
options.b: That the reward should be larger
options.c: Collision checking for the vehicle footprint and relevant motion constraints
options.d: That A* should always be replaced by PPO

questions.explanation: A point path does not account for the occupied area of a vehicle. The collision model and motion constraints must match the intended vehicle approximation.

questions.question_text: A PPO planner has higher average training reward than a rule-based baseline. Which next result best supports a driving-performance comparison?

options.a: Only the single most visually impressive rollout
options.c: Reward measured again on the same training scenarios
options.d: Matched held-out scenarios with separate collision, completion, and travel-time results for both planners

questions.explanation: Reward can be improved in ways that do not improve safety or task completion. Comparable evaluation conditions and distinct outcome measures expose those trade-offs.

# Welcome

Planning is the layer that decides what the car actually does. Perception tells you what is there; control tells you how to move. Planning is everything in between, and it is where most of the genuinely hard decisions live.

## What you will build

A planning stack, in layers:

- **Global planning** — route-level search across the road network
- **Behaviour planning with an FSM** — follow, overtake, yield
- **Local planning with a lattice planner** — turning a decision into a drivable trajectory
- **End-to-end planning with RL (PPO)** — a learned planner with no hand-written rules
- **Closed-loop ML planners** — learned planners judged in the loop, not on a log
- **Motion prediction** — what everything else is about to do
- **MPDM** — deciding by simulating candidate policies forward

## Why the order matters

Route, behaviour, trajectory. That decomposition is how essentially every production autonomy stack is organised, and you build each layer before seeing them compose. Then you replace the whole thing with a learned planner and argue about which was better.

**Start with Traditional Motion Planning.**

You have built the planning stack twice — once classically, once learned — and you should now be able to argue for either without hand-waving.

additions.content_value:
# Perception lab: measure geometry before trusting a scene model

Use this guide with the existing playground link, lecture, and slides. It supplies a small experiment that runs independently of playground access and gives you numbers against which to check your intuition. The purpose is to connect pixels, geometric assumptions, and evaluation evidence before moving to richer semantic, motion, reconstruction, and generative examples.

## Prerequisites and study sequence

You need Python 3, arithmetic with ratios, and the ability to read a short function. No downloaded model, GPU, camera, or private dataset is required for the synthetic exercise. Use your own local notebook or a blank Colab notebook and retain its code and outputs.

Start at the module overview and identify a question you can measure. Study the lecture and slides alongside the playground rather than treating an interactive result as its own explanation. Work through camera projection first, stereo geometry second, and error sensitivity third. Then choose one semantic or motion experiment and document its input, output, units, and reference data.

Write coordinate conventions at the top of the notebook: image coordinates `(u, v)` in pixels; camera coordinates `(X, Y, Z)` in meters; positive `Z` in front of the camera. The [OpenCV calibration documentation](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html) defines the pinhole relationship and separates intrinsics, pose, and lens distortion. The exercise below assumes an ideal distortion-free pair with identical intrinsics and parallel optical axes.

## Runnable exercise: projection, disparity, and depth

Save as `camera_lab.py` and run `python3 camera_lab.py`. Focal length is 800 pixels, horizontal principal point is 320 pixels, vertical principal point is 240 pixels, and stereo baseline is 0.20 meters.

```python
from math import isclose

F, CX, CY, BASELINE = 800.0, 320.0, 240.0, 0.20

def project(x, y, z):
    if z <= 0:
        raise ValueError('Point must be in front of the camera')
    return F*x/z + CX, F*y/z + CY

def depth(disparity):
    if disparity <= 0:
        raise ValueError('Use a valid positive disparity in this setup')
    return F*BASELINE/disparity

left = project(1.0, 0.0, 4.0)
right = project(1.0-BASELINE, 0.0, 4.0)
disparity = left[0]-right[0]
assert left == (520.0, 240.0)
assert right == (480.0, 240.0)
assert isclose(depth(disparity), 4.0)
assert isclose(depth(20.0), 8.0)
for invalid in (0.0, -1.0):
    try:
        depth(invalid)
        raise AssertionError('Invalid disparity was accepted')
    except ValueError:
        pass
print('left:', left, 'right:', right)
for d in (40.0, 20.0, 10.0):
    print(f'd={d:.0f}px, Z={depth(d):.3f}m, +1px error={depth(d+1)-depth(d):.3f}m')
```

The first pair must project to `(520, 240)` and `(480, 240)`, giving a disparity of 40 pixels and depth of 4 meters. The final three lines should show depths of 4, 8, and 16 meters; a positive one-pixel disparity error changes them by approximately −0.098, −0.381, and −1.455 meters respectively. The same pixel error becomes more consequential at smaller disparities. These are results of this constructed geometry, not measured camera accuracy.

Repeat with half the focal length and predict the projected point before running it. Then halve image resolution: scale focal length and principal point consistently. Keep baseline in meters. Deliberately use 20 as the baseline while still labeling it meters and observe the hundredfold depth error. This is a unit test for your reasoning, not a way to estimate an unknown physical baseline.

## Failure cases to record

The simple depth formula assumes rectified correspondence with this disparity convention. Textureless regions, occlusions, repeated patterns, bad matching, and unsynchronized motion can invalidate the correspondence. Zero disparity should remain invalid or unbounded in your report, never silently become a nearby obstacle. A negative disparity needs inspection of conventions and validity before interpretation.

Projection also changes when intrinsics are wrong, lens distortion is ignored, or a world-frame point is used as if it were already in the camera frame. Measure error at the image edges as well as the center when extending the exercise to calibration. Keep some calibration images aside for evaluation; fitting a pattern is different from showing performance on an unseen view.

## Add a semantic or motion check

For a semantic extension, compare two axis-aligned boxes: reference `(10,10,30,30)` and prediction `(20,10,40,30)`, using continuous corner coordinates. Intersection area is 200, union is 600, and IoU is one third. Explain how the outcome changes when a small object shifts by the same number of pixels. A single box overlap does not establish detector precision, recall, or dataset performance.

For motion, track a synthetic point from `(100,100)` to `(110,100)` over 0.1 seconds. Its image displacement is 10 pixels and image velocity is 100 pixels/second. This does not establish meters/second without additional geometry. The [OpenCV tracking reference](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/dc/d6b/group__video__track.html) provides optical-flow functions for a later real-image extension.

When exploring reconstruction or generation, distinguish appearance from geometric evidence. The [NeRF paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934) addresses novel-view synthesis from posed images; a convincing generated view alone does not validate obstacle distance or free space. Describe exactly what evidence your chosen task supplies to a downstream planner.

## Capstone and evaluation rubric

Submit one notebook containing the executable geometry exercise, a parameter sweep, one deliberately broken assumption, and a semantic or motion extension. Award 30% for correct frames, units, and numeric checks; 25% for controlled experiments and an interpretable result table; 25% for failure analysis with a justified validity mask or rejected result; and 20% for reproducibility and clear limitations. Include screenshots only as supporting evidence. Your conclusion should identify which perception quantity you measured, its reference, and what remains unknown before using it in a driving system.

questions.question_text: For the lab’s ideal rectified stereo pair, focal length is 800 pixels, baseline is 0.20 meters, and disparity is 20 pixels. What depth follows from Z = fB/d?
questions.explanation: The units of pixels cancel: (800 pixels × 0.20 meters) / 20 pixels = 8 meters. The formula depends on valid rectified correspondence and the stated disparity convention.

questions.question_text: An image is resized to half its original width and height with no crop. How should its pinhole intrinsics be adjusted for the resized pixel coordinates?

options.a: Halve focal lengths and principal-point coordinates; keep the physical stereo baseline unchanged
options.c: Leave focal lengths and principal point unchanged

questions.explanation: Focal lengths and principal-point coordinates are expressed in pixels, so uniform image scaling changes them. Resizing the image does not move the physical cameras.

questions.question_text: A tracked point moves 10 pixels horizontally in 0.1 seconds. What can be concluded directly?

options.a: The object moved at 100 meters per second
options.b: Its image velocity is 100 pixels per second; metric velocity needs additional geometry and assumptions
options.d: The camera must have remained stationary

questions.explanation: Pixel displacement divided by time gives image velocity. It does not by itself separate object motion from camera motion or establish metric scale.

questions.question_text: A novel generated view looks realistic. What evidence is still needed before treating its apparent free space as a geometric measurement?

options.d: A relevant geometric reference and an evaluation of distance or occupancy error for the intended task

questions.explanation: Visual plausibility is not a measurement of metric depth or occupancy. Validate the quantity the downstream planner actually needs against an appropriate reference.
